A channel is a typed conduit through which one goroutine hands a value to another, and the handover is the synchronisation point rather than a side effect of it.
Every channel carries an element type, so the compiler rejects a send whose value cannot be received on the other side.
An unbuffered channel completes a send only when a receiver is ready, which is why it doubles as a rendezvous between two goroutines. The buffered form relaxes that by admitting a fixed number of queued values.
Capacity is fixed when the channel is made and never changes afterwards, so a program cannot grow a queue to absorb a burst it did not plan for.
Receiving from a closed channel yields the zero value of the element type immediately, and the two value form reports whether the value was real.
Closing is a sender side operation. A receiver that closes a channel invites a send on a closed channel, which is a run time panic rather than an error value.
A nil channel blocks forever on both operations, which is occasionally useful as a way to disable one arm of a select without restructuring the loop. The select statement is where that behaviour pays off.
Select chooses among ready cases uniformly at random, so a program must not depend on the order in which its cases were written.
A default case turns select into a non blocking probe, and it is the usual way to attempt a send without risking a stall.
Directional channel types narrow a parameter to send only or receive only, which documents intent and lets the compiler enforce it.
The runtime detects the case where every goroutine is blocked on channel operations and reports a deadlock rather than hanging silently.
Two rules cover most channel bugs in practice:
  • the goroutine that owns a channel is the one that closes it
  • a receiver never assumes a value arrived without checking the second result
Neither rule is enforced by the compiler, so both belong in review rather than in the type system.
